steps.tx: A **closed ICU** is one in which the intensivist writes the orders. Observational comparisons link and associate that model with better outcomes. An **open unit**, where every parent team writes its own critical care, fragments the plan. A title on the door, without the authority to change the ventilator, is not a closed unit.

steps.tx: The **MERIT** trial introduced a **medical emergency team** and did not significantly reduce the composite of cardiac arrest, unplanned ICU admission, and unexpected death. Calling criteria are still widely used. The trial is a reason not to claim a mortality benefit it did not show. Rapid response systems improve timely clinical evaluation even if trial endpoints remained neutral.

steps.tx: A **NEWS2** total of 7 or more is the high-risk band and needs an emergency response. A score of 3 in one parameter needs urgent review even when the total looks moderate. **Scale 2**, for a patient at risk of **hypercapnic respiratory failure**, sets the oxygen saturation target at 88 to 92 percent. Scale 1 is the default.

left.title: NEWS2 risk bands
points: Score 0 to 4: Low clinical risk; ward-level monitoring
Score 5 to 6 or individual score 3: Medium risk; urgent review
Score 7 or greater: High clinical risk; emergency ICU response

right.title: Scale 2 oxygen saturation
points: Applied in confirmed chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure
Prevents unwarranted alarms from controlled physiological hypoxaemia

steps.tx: In the NHSN framework a **ventilator-associated condition** is a rise in the daily minimum FiO2 of 0.20 or more, or in PEEP of 3 cmH2O or more, sustained for 2 calendar days after a stable baseline. An **infection-related ventilator-associated complication** adds abnormal temperature or white cell count and a new antibiotic. This is surveillance. It is not the same as a clinical pneumonia, and it is not by itself a reason to start antibiotics.

rows: FiO2 rise >= 0.20 or PEEP rise >= 3 cmH2O for 2 days
VAC criteria plus fever or leucocytosis plus new antibiotic
Identifies pulmonary or extrapulmonary infectious triggers
Does not equate to microbiological ventilator pneumonia

steps.tx: The **Michigan Keystone programme** used a **central-line checklist** and a rule that any member of the team could stop the procedure when a step was missed. Catheter bloodstream infections fell. It was a collaborative, not a randomised trial. The steps remain hand hygiene, chlorhexidine, a full barrier, a safer site, and removal of the line.

left.title: Keystone ICU bundle
points: Strict hand hygiene prior to catheter placement
Chlorhexidine skin antisepsis with adequate drying time
Full-barrier sterile draping and subclavian site preference

right.title: Safety culture empowerment
points: Bedside nurses empowered to halt non-compliant procedures
Dramatic sustained reduction in catheter bloodstream infections
Daily audit ensuring prompt removal of unneeded lines

steps.tx: Structured handover is conducted using **ISBAR**: identity, situation, background, assessment, and recommendation. A list of drugs with no plan loses the sickest problem. The incoming clinician repeats that problem back. Standardizing structured clinical communication during multidisciplinary shift transitions eliminates information omissions and reduces preventable medical errors.

steps.tx: **Tele-ICU** lets an intensivist review a remote unit and support the local nurse and doctor. It does not see the skin, the family, or a displaced tube as well as the person at the bedside. The **bedside check** still happens. Remote audio-visual monitoring expands specialist access across community hospitals but cannot replace direct physical examination.

left.title: Tele-ICU capabilities
points: Centralized specialist oversight of physiological trends
Early identification of clinical deterioration markers

right.title: Bedside care primacy
points: Direct tactile physical examination and tube security
Immediate hands-on procedural interventions and airway rescue

steps.tx: A **daily goals sheet** states the sedation target, the ventilation plan, the feeding plan, and which lines and drugs can stop. A **pharmacist on the round** catches dose errors. These are safety practices, not paperwork for its own sake. Structured multidisciplinary rounds streamline clinical workflows and optimize patient outcomes.
